clue.text: Office enjoys short meal quickly

indicators.note: A short version of a word is that word stopped before its end, so the meal named next arrives a letter down.

parts.note: a post is an office in the sense of a position held — the post of treasurer
to enjoy good health or a fine view is to have it
tea is a meal in Britain as well as a drink, and it comes up one letter short

explanation.surface: A government department hurrying through a quick bite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Office' looks like the place stamps are sold and means a position held instead. Tea is the British evening meal, eaten early, which is what lets a drink be clued as food.
explanation.definitionFit: Post-haste was the old instruction written on urgent mail — carry this at the speed of the post — and it survives as an adverb meaning at top speed.

clue.text: Never finishing, choose appropriate meal

indicators.note: Neither of the two words that follow is allowed to finish, so each is written without its final letter.

parts.note: to choose is to pick, and the k is never reached
to appropriate something is to nick it, British slang for helping yourself, and again the k is never reached

explanation.surface: Somebody who can never decide settling on a suitable lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriate' reads as the adjective beside it — a suitable meal — and is the verb, to help yourself to something. One instruction governs both words at once, which is what hides the join.
explanation.definitionFit: A picnic is a meal carried out of doors and eaten off a rug, so the plain word meal covers it.

clue.text: Shy type treating fellow winner like Mike Teavee?

indicators.note: To treat one person like another is to do to them what was done to the other, so the boy's fate becomes a description and goes in front of the girl.

parts.note: in Roald Dahl's Charlie and the Chocolate Factory Mike Teavee is sent through a television camera and comes out a few inches tall
the gum-chewing girl who swells into a blueberry holds another of the five golden tickets, and her first name is wanted

explanation.surface: A bashful child putting a fellow prizewinner through what the television-mad boy suffered.
explanation.walkthrough: Both children are golden-ticket winners in the same book, so one name and one fate can be joined without the surface creaking. The question mark admits the whole thing rests on remembering Dahl.
explanation.definitionFit: A shrinking violet is the everyday English phrase for a retiring, self-effacing person, the one who will not come forward.

clue.text: Very fine ventilation policy introduced by hospital

indicators.note: Whoever introduces a thing goes on ahead of it, so the letter for the place named afterwards heads the answer.

parts.note: h = hospital, the letter on the road sign pointing to one
ventilation is the moving of air through a building
a policy is a line, as in the party line or taking a hard line

explanation.surface: A hospital bringing in a new rule about keeping the wards ventilated.
explanation.walkthrough: A hairline crack is one no wider than a single hair, which is how the noun came to serve as an adjective. 'Policy' meaning an official position is a sense setters return to constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairline fracture is one as narrow as a hair, so hairline describes anything very fine indeed.

clue.text: Frisky agent holding hands?

indicators.note: What is held is held inside, so the agent opens after two letters and everything else goes in the gap.

parts.note: a spy is an agent in the espionage sense the surface wants
the two hands are the right one spelt out and l, the usual letter for left

explanation.surface: A lively secret agent keeping hold of somebody's hands.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is apologising for the two hands being treated unequally: one written out in full, the other cut to its single letter. Sprightly is used of energy nobody expected, usually in the elderly.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprightly means brisk and full of life, which is what frisky says of anything lively on its feet.

clue.text: Tall bird among others on time

parts.note: eg picks out one case from several others, the tag for an example
re means on the subject of, as at the head of a memo
t = time, the letter in every physics formula

explanation.surface: A wading bird standing punctually about with the rest of the flock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' is the trap: in a down clue it usually says where a piece sits, and here it is a piece in its own right. The bird is the white heron of estuaries and rice fields, which is where the height comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: An egret is a slender white heron, long in the neck and leg, so tall is how it stands at the water's edge.

clue.text: Nut packers agreed to include high grade plant fibre

indicators.note: What a firm includes it takes inside itself, so the grade named next drops in among the packers' letters.

parts.note: KP Snacks is the British firm whose peanuts are sold in every pub as KP Nuts
ok is the everyday word for agreed
a is the top grade on a school report

explanation.surface: A snack company signing off on some top-quality raw material.
explanation.walkthrough: A brand name is doing the heavy lifting, and it means nothing unless you have walked past a British crisp aisle. Kapok is the silky floss round the seeds of the ceiba tree, once the standard stuffing for life jackets.
explanation.definitionFit: Kapok is the light, water-repellent fibre taken from the seed pods of the kapok tree and used to stuff cushions and mattresses.

clue.text: Pure in faith, that woman bears heavy blows

indicators.note: A load rests on the shoulders of whoever bears it, so in this downward entry the woman goes underneath what she is carrying.

parts.note: a ko is a knockout, the blow that finishes a fight, and the plural adds the s
her is the pronoun for the woman already mentioned

explanation.surface: A devout woman putting up with a battering.
explanation.walkthrough: Kosher food satisfies Jewish dietary law, and the word has spread into general English for anything above board. In a down clue the bearer is below the burden, which is what settles the order.
explanation.definitionFit: Kosher food is prepared according to Jewish dietary law, so the word means ritually clean — pure in the eyes of the faith.

clue.text: High diver losing day in terrible career-ending flop

indicators.note: What is lost is not there to be used, so the day's letter goes missing from the pile before anything else happens to it.
Something terrible is in a dreadful state, and letters in a dreadful state are no longer standing in the order they were written.

parts.note: anagram fodder, sixteen letters
d = day, and it is the letter dropped before the rearranging

explanation.surface: A disastrous performance that brought somebody's working life to an end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High diver' is the definition and reads as one more detail of the flop, which is why it disappears into the sentence. The bird hunts by stooping, and has been clocked above 200mph doing it.
explanation.definitionFit: A peregrine kills by folding its wings and dropping on prey from a great height, which makes it the highest diver in nature.

clue.text: King with deer in sight shows years of education

definitions.note: The definition is plural where the answer is singular: one key stage is a named block of school years, so the setter names it by the several it covers.

parts.note: k = king, the chess notation and the playing card

indicators.note: What is in a thing sits inside it, so the animal named just before drops into the middle of the word for sight.

parts.note: the eye is the organ of sight, and it is the word that gets opened up
a stag is a male deer

explanation.surface: A monarch out stalking, with a deer in his sights.
explanation.walkthrough: English schools are divided into key stages, blocks of school years tested together — the first runs from age five to seven — so the definition is the official term, not a loose phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The national curriculum in England groups school years into key stages, each ending in national tests, so one of them is a span of years of education.

clue.text: Woman in Number 10 once, remembered primarily for bag?

parts.note: Number 10 Downing Street is the British Prime Minister's house, and Boris Johnson's wife lived there with him; her first name is wanted

indicators.note: Primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of the word before it is taken.

parts.note: its opening letter and nothing else of the word

explanation.surface: A former resident of Downing Street chiefly recalled for her handbag.
explanation.walkthrough: The handbag points hard at Margaret Thatcher, whose one is a national memory, and the woman wanted is the far more recent Mrs Johnson. In British shops a carrier is what you are charged a few pence for at the till.
explanation.definitionFit: A carrier is the shortened everyday name for a carrier bag, the plastic or paper one a shop hands over.

clue.text: Fresh out of clothing may I ask for new coat?

indicators.note: The clothing of a word is the letter at either end of it, and out of takes both off, leaving the middle standing bare.

parts.note: the five-letter word with the letter at each end stripped away
pray is the old polite way of asking — what, pray, is this?

explanation.surface: Somebody with nothing left to wear asking for a new coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fresh out of' reads as the idiom for having run out of something, and the two words do quite different jobs here: one is the material, the other the instruction. The coat wanted is a coat of paint.
explanation.definitionFit: A respray puts a fresh coat of paint on a car, so a new coat is exactly what it is once you stop thinking about clothes.

clue.text: Somewhere to stay during November

parts.note: in means during — in the war, in the night
november is the radio alphabet's word for n

explanation.surface: Finding a bed for the night somewhere in the middle of November.
explanation.walkthrough: November is a month everywhere except in the radio alphabet, where it is only ever a letter. Three-letter answers lean on that sort of shorthand almost every time.
explanation.definitionFit: An inn is a public house with rooms to let, so somewhere to stay is what it offers a traveller.

clue.text: Less beefy women's crew on land

indicators.note: In an across entry a thing placed on another is written after it, so the crew clued first ends up at the back.

parts.note: to light on a branch is to land on it, the verb that survives in alight
w = women, the letter on the lavatory door
an eight is the rowing crew of that number, the boat the Boat Race is won in

explanation.surface: A women's rowing crew doing their training on dry land.
explanation.walkthrough: Rowing supplies the whole surface, and lightweight is a genuine racing category with a weight limit for the crew. 'Land' is the verb, to come down and settle, not the ground underfoot.
explanation.definitionFit: A lightweight is the boxing or rowing division below the heavier ones, so as a description it means slight rather than beefy.

clue.text: Early Jesuit outfit an American soldier brought back

indicators.note: Bringing a thing back turns it round, and in an across entry that means the assembly is read from its right-hand end.

parts.note: an outfit is a set of clothes, the sort with a jacket and trousers
the article taken exactly as it stands
a GI is an American private, from the government issue stamped on his kit

explanation.surface: A religious order's first habit, carried home by an American serviceman.
explanation.walkthrough: Ignatius Loyola was a Basque soldier invalided out of the army before he founded the Society of Jesus in 1540, so the soldier in the wordplay is a quiet joke. 'Outfit' points at a religious order and means clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignatius Loyola founded the Jesuits and served as their first superior general, which makes him the earliest Jesuit there was.

clue.text: Football team having gone up finished without improvement

indicators.note: A club that has gone up has been promoted, and in a down entry going up means its letters are read from the foot of the space towards the top.

parts.note: Man U is Manchester United, and this down entry takes the name upwards
something finished has ended

explanation.surface: A promoted side that has finished the season no better than it began.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having gone up' works twice over: promotion is what football clubs do, and a down answer is the one place letters can travel upwards. Man U is the universal shorthand for Manchester United.
explanation.definitionFit: An unamended text is one nobody has corrected, so it stands exactly as it was — without improvement.

clue.text: Honk in MG, taking the car outside

indicators.note: The car is the two letters just named, and taking them outside wraps them round the little word before them.

parts.note: MG is the British sports-car marque, the octagonal badge on an open two-seater
the word in, taken exactly as it stands

explanation.surface: Sounding the horn from inside an MG.
explanation.walkthrough: Honk and ming are both British slang for a foul smell — it mings is northern and Scottish — and honking a horn is the reading the surface wants. No synonym is needed anywhere: the clue works on the two words as printed.
explanation.definitionFit: To ming is to stink, and to honk is the same slang: both are everyday British for something that smells foul.

clue.text: Watchtower article starts with insult and ends in mini panegyric

indicators.note: What a thing starts with comes first, so the insult is written at the front of the article.

parts.note: a barb is a cutting remark

indicators.note: An end is a last letter, and this takes the final one of each of the two words that follow.

parts.note: the closing letter of each of these two words, in the order they are given
an is the indefinite article, written out in full rather than abbreviated

explanation.surface: A magazine piece that opens with an insult and finishes on a short burst of praise.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics turn Watchtower into a title — the Jehovah's Witnesses' magazine — so it reads as where the article appeared, and it is the definition. A panegyric is a speech of elaborate praise.
explanation.definitionFit: A barbican is the fortified outwork guarding a castle or town gate, towered so that the approach to it can be watched.

clue.text: Some pressure building across stream, perhaps obstruction limiting current

indicators.note: To limit a thing is to set a bound on each side of it, so the single letter for the current is shut in between the two words around it.

parts.note: a watermill is built over the stream that drives its wheel, and perhaps admits it is only one such building
a bar laid across a way is an obstruction
i is the physicist's symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: Water pressure building behind something blocking the flow of a stream.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word of the surface is about water — stream, current, pressure building — and the current in the wordplay is the electrical one. Weather charts still give air pressure in millibars, a thousandth of a bar each.
explanation.definitionFit: A millibar is the unit atmospheric pressure is measured in on a forecaster's chart, so it is a quantity of pressure.

clue.text: Simple liver in water left in oven

indicators.note: Left is put in the oven, and what goes in a thing sits inside it, between its letters.

parts.note: an Aga is the cast-iron range that sits in the kitchen of many an English farmhouse
l = left, the letter used on plans and stage directions

explanation.surface: A liver kept in water and then left sitting in the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Simple liver' means something that lives simply, not an organ — algae have no root, stem or leaf between them. An Aga is a make of range so common in Britain that the brand does duty for the thing.
explanation.definitionFit: An alga is the simplest form of water plant, from pond scum to seaweed, living in water with none of the parts a land plant needs.

clue.text: Man upset with deity destroying stuff

indicators.note: Something upset has been knocked over and its contents spilled, so the letters no longer lie in the order they were set down.

parts.note: anagram fodder, three letters
anagram fodder, five more

explanation.surface: A man who has fallen out with his god and is smashing the place up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Destroying' looks exactly like a shuffle instruction and belongs to the definition; the small word before the god is what does the work. Read as two words, destroying stuff is material that destroys.
explanation.definitionFit: Dynamite is the nitroglycerine explosive Nobel patented, so it is literally stuff for destroying things with.

clue.text: Ill guy trembles in a bad way

indicators.note: Something trembling will not hold still, so its letters cannot be relied on to stay where they were put.

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.surface: A sick man shaking with fever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a bad way' is also the idiom for being seriously ill, which is why it settles so quietly beside the ill guy. It has to name a manner rather than a quality, because the answer is an adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: Uglily is the adverb from ugly — done in an ugly manner — and an ugly manner is a bad way to do a thing.

clue.text: Refuse some fake generosity, returning it

indicators.note: Some of a thing is a part of it, so what is wanted is a run of letters already written out rather than the words themselves.
What returns comes back over its own path, so the run has to be read the other way about.

parts.note: the run starts at the end of the first word and stops inside the second, and it arrives facing the wrong way
the gift being handed back in the surface, and no part of the letters

explanation.surface: Turning down a gift that was never meant kindly, and handing it back.
explanation.walkthrough: To renege is to go back on an undertaking, and the letters are buried going backwards in a phrase about giving something back — the sense and the mechanism are pulling the same way. A hidden word this long in a six-letter answer leaves almost nothing for the solver to build on.
explanation.definitionFit: To renege on an agreement is to refuse to honour it, so refuse is the verb it stands in for.

clue.text: Fish follows Brighton swimming master

indicators.note: Letters set swimming are adrift and can come ashore in any order at all.
What follows a thing comes along behind it, so the fish named first is written last.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters; Brighton is the big resort on the English south coast
the eel is the crossword's default fish, and it comes through unshuffled

explanation.surface: An eel trailing a swimming instructor through the water off Brighton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Master' is placed to be read with the word before it — a swimming master is what a school calls its instructor — and it is the definition, and a verb. The seaside keeps the anagram indicator looking like scenery.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring a dog to heel is to make it walk obediently at your side, so to bring a person to heel is to master them.

clue.text: Brown ring lifted in unpleasant job

indicators.note: Lifted means raised, and in a down entry raising a letter carries it out of the middle of its word and up to the top.

parts.note: a ring is drawn as the letter o
an unpleasant job is a chore, and this is what it has left once the ring has gone up

explanation.surface: A brown ring hoisted out of a thoroughly dirty job.
explanation.walkthrough: Ochre is the iron-rich clay ground for pigment since the cave paintings, which is where its yellow-brown comes from. Only a down clue can ask for a letter to be lifted; across, it would have to be dragged.
explanation.definitionFit: Ochre is the earthy iron pigment of cave paintings and it names that colour, a brown carrying a good deal of yellow.

clue.text: Mischievous goddess visiting Earth

parts.note: to be visiting somewhere is to be at it
e = earth, the letter marking the third pin of a British plug

explanation.surface: A goddess coming down to see how the mortals are getting along.
explanation.walkthrough: Ate is the Greek goddess of ruin and reckless folly, the one who blinds people into their worst decisions. Earth here is the wiring diagram's earth, not the planet the surface is pointing at.
explanation.definitionFit: Ate is the Greek goddess of delusion and mischief, who lures people into the folly that ruins them.

clue.text: Pass food on its way to being frozen?

definitions.text: on its way to being frozen

parts.note: a col is the saddle between two peaks, the dip a mountain pass goes through
a dish is a prepared food, one item off a menu

explanation.surface: Handing the plates round before the meal loses its heat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass' reads as the polite request at table and means a gap in the mountains. The definition is a joke about the ending: -ish stops short of the thing itself, so the temperature is only heading that way.
explanation.definitionFit: Coldish is cold without committing to it, so it describes something part of the way towards frozen and no further.

clue.text: Returning European sent a telegram, having left late in fiasco

indicators.note: Something returning comes back the way it went, so in an across entry the assembly is read from its right-hand end.
It says where the borrowed letter is wanted: not in the place it came from but near the finish of the word.

parts.note: e = European, the letter on a passport or a car plate
to cable was to send a telegram, and this is that word once the letter below has been taken out of it
l = left, and it has left the telegram word to go in further on

explanation.surface: A European who wired ahead and then set off too late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having left' is doing two jobs at once, the departure in the surface and the letter for left, pulled out of the telegram word to go back in nearer the end. Cable as a verb belongs to the age of the transatlantic telegraph.
explanation.definitionFit: A debacle is a sudden and humiliating collapse of something that was meant to work, which is what a fiasco is.

clue.text: Smart abstaining in negative vote

indicators.note: What goes in a thing sits inside it, so the abstainers land between the letters of the vote.

parts.note: nay is the negative called in a parliamentary division
tt is teetotal, said of somebody who abstains from drink

explanation.surface: A well-turned-out member declining to support the motion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abstaining' looks parliamentary, sitting where it does beside a vote, and means off the drink altogether. Smart in British English is about dress before it is about brains.
explanation.definitionFit: Natty means neatly and stylishly turned out — a natty suit, a natty dresser — which is smart in the clothes sense.

clue.text: Nun cared about English patient suffering

indicators.note: Things scattered about a place are lying anywhere, and letters lying anywhere have lost the order they were given in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
e = English, joining the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A nun looking after an ailing Englishman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patient' reads as the sick man in the bed and is an adjective in the definition. The English Patient sits right there in the surface, which makes the misreading almost automatic.
explanation.definitionFit: Endurance is the capacity to bear pain or hardship without giving way, which is patient suffering exactly.
